words.definition: A ruler who holds absolute power and often wields it cruelly or unfairly.
words.example: The despot jailed anyone who dared to criticize a single one of his decrees.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'the spot' — a despot puts every rival on the spot, then removes them.

words.definition: A cruel, oppressive ruler who governs harshly and ignores the rights of others.
words.example: Under the tyrant, families whispered indoors, terrified their words would reach his spies.
words.mnemonic: 'TYRE-ant' — picture a giant ant that flattens everyone beneath it like a rolling tire.

words.definition: One person who governs a country with unlimited authority and no checks or restraints.
words.example: The autocrat abolished parliament and began making every state decision entirely alone.
words.mnemonic: 'auto' (self) + 'crat' (rule) = self-rule; an 'automatic' ruler who runs everything himself.

words.definition: A powerful monarch or leader who commands wide authority over a realm or people.
words.example: Robed in gold, the potentate received tribute from a dozen conquered provinces.
words.mnemonic: 'potent' + '-ate' — a potentate is a potent leader brimming with power.

words.definition: Ruling in a harsh, controlling way that permits no freedom or dissent.
words.example: His despotic management meant no employee dared question even a trivial order.
words.mnemonic: 'de-SPOT-ic' — think of a boss who spots your every move and controls it.

words.definition: Taking every decision alone and demanding obedience without consulting anyone else.
words.example: The autocratic coach benched any player who offered even a mild suggestion.
words.mnemonic: 'auto' = self; such a leader acts on 'automatic,' never asking others first.

words.definition: Using power in a cruel, unjust, and heavily controlling manner over others.
words.example: Her tyrannical stepmother assigned endless chores and forbade even a moment of rest.
words.mnemonic: 'TYRE-annical' — imagine tires rolling cruelly over anyone who gets in the way.

words.definition: Constantly bossing other people and insisting on always getting your own way.
words.example: His domineering mother chose his clothes, his friends, and even his career.
words.mnemonic: 'domi-NEER-ing' — picture someone leaning ('nearing') over you, ruling your whole domain.

words.definition: Forcing your opinions on others in a pushy, arrogant, and unpleasant way.
words.example: The overbearing host wouldn't let a single guest refuse a third helping of food.
words.mnemonic: 'over-bearing' — imagine a heavy bear leaning over you, its weight impossible to escape.

words.definition: Demanding strict, total obedience and allowing people very little personal freedom.
words.example: The authoritarian regime banned all protests and censored every newspaper in the country.
words.mnemonic: Spot 'author' inside it — one who insists on being the sole 'author' of every rule you follow.

words.definition: Bossing everyone through absolute power and tolerating no disagreement whatsoever.
words.example: The dictatorial director rewrote the entire script and ignored the writers' protests.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'dictate' — such a person dictates orders that everyone is forced to obey.

words.definition: Holding leading power or influence over other groups, states, or ideas.
words.example: For decades one hegemonic superpower dictated the terms of global trade.
words.mnemonic: 'he-GEM-onic' — picture a nation clutching a giant gem that gives it power over all rivals.

words.definition: Supreme power to govern, or the territory held under one ruler's control.
words.example: The empire's dominion stretched from the icy north to the desert south.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'dominus' (lord) — a dominion is the domain where the lord holds sway.

words.definition: A nation's supreme power to govern itself, free from any outside control.
words.example: After the long war, the small country finally regained its sovereignty.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'reign' — it is the reign a people hold over their own land.

words.definition: Having supreme, independent power and answering to no higher authority.
words.example: Each sovereign nation sets its own laws without seeking permission from its neighbors.
words.mnemonic: 'sovereign' hides 'reign' — a sovereign state reigns supreme over itself.

words.definition: The relationship in which a dominant nation controls a weaker one's external affairs while allowing local self-rule.
words.example: Under the empire's suzerainty, the small kingdom ran its own villages but could sign no treaties alone.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'sooze-rain-tee' — picture a superior power making authority 'rain' down over lands it doesn't fully own; from French 'sus' = above.

words.definition: The condition of being completely under another's power, or a person held in bondage.
words.example: Held in thrall by the cult leader, she obeyed his every command without question.
words.mnemonic: Thrall lives inside 'enthrall' — being so captivated that you are effectively held captive; Old Norse 'þræll' meant slave.

words.definition: A feudal tenant who received land from a lord in exchange for allegiance and military service.
words.example: The vassal knelt before his lord, pledging his sword in return for the manor he had been granted.
words.mnemonic: Vassal sounds like 'vessel' — a vessel that holds a lord's land and carries out his will.

words.definition: A farm laborer bound to a manor and its owner during the feudal era.
words.example: The serf could not leave the estate; he tilled the same fields his father had worked.
words.mnemonic: Serf sounds like 'serve' — a worker tied to the soil he must forever serve.

words.definition: To conquer a people or group and force them into obedience.
words.example: The general vowed to subjugate the rebellious province and crush any resistance.
words.mnemonic: Sub + jugum (Latin 'yoke') — to put someone 'under the yoke,' like an ox forced to plow.

words.definition: To force a person into bondage and total loss of freedom.
words.example: Colonizers sought to enslave the native population, forcing them to labor without pay or rights.
words.mnemonic: The prefix 'en-' means 'to make' — picture chains snapping onto someone the instant the word begins.

words.definition: To keep people down through cruel and unjust use of power.
words.example: The regime used censorship and secret police to oppress anyone who dared to speak out.
words.mnemonic: Op- + press (Latin 'opprimere,' to press against) — to press down hard on people until they can't rise.

words.definition: Harshly controlling and unjust, or so heavy that it weighs one down.
words.example: Life under the oppressive dictatorship left citizens afraid to gather or even whisper complaints.
words.mnemonic: Think 'op-press' — anything that presses down on you, whether a cruel ruler or a stifling summer day.

words.definition: To rule over or treat others with cruel, unchecked harshness.
words.example: The older boys tyrannized the younger students, taking their lunch money and mocking them daily.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'tyranno-' as in Tyrannosaurus — picture a T-Rex stomping on everyone below it.

words.definition: Cruel, unjust government by a single ruler who holds absolute power.
words.example: The revolution was fought to end centuries of tyranny under kings who answered to no one.
words.mnemonic: 'Tyranno-' like the T-Rex — one giant beast ruling by fear and teeth.

words.definition: To force a person into acting by using threats, pressure, or intimidation.
words.example: They tried to coerce the witness into silence by threatening her family.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'co-force' — forcing someone along with you against their will; Latin 'coercere' = to restrain.

words.definition: The act of forcing someone to comply by using threats or intimidation.
words.example: The confession was thrown out because it was obtained through coercion, not free choice.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'co-force-ion' — the noun for applying force to bend someone's will.

words.definition: To drive or force someone to act, often by pressure or strong influence.
words.example: A sense of duty compelled her to report the crime, even though she feared retaliation.
words.mnemonic: Com- + 'pel' (Latin 'pellere,' to drive) — the same 'pel' as in propel and expel: to drive someone forward.

words.definition: To hold back or limit what someone is able to do.
words.example: Tight budgets constrained the team, forcing them to cut features they had promised.
words.mnemonic: Con- + 'strain' — picture a tight strap or strain that binds you and holds you back; Latin 'stringere' = to bind tight.

words.definition: To hold power over others or be the most powerful force in a situation.
words.example: The champion dominated every match, winning so easily her opponents seemed barely present.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'dominus' (lord/master) — the same root as 'dome' towering above everything below it.

words.definition: The state of having controlling power or influence over others.
words.example: The lion asserted its dominance over the pride by defeating every challenger.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'dominoes' — the piece that stays standing knocks all the others flat.

words.definition: Ranked below another in importance, power, or authority.
words.example: As a subordinate, she reported to three managers who all outranked her.
words.mnemonic: 'sub-' (under) + 'ordinate' (order) — placed under others in the pecking order.

words.definition: Overly eager to obey and serve someone, often to an embarrassing degree.
words.example: The waiter's subservient bowing and scraping made the guests squirm.
words.mnemonic: 'sub-' (under) + 'serve' — you stand under someone, endlessly serving them.

words.definition: Tending to yield meekly to the control or authority of others.
words.example: The new recruit stayed submissive, never once questioning an order.
words.mnemonic: 'sub-' (under) + 'missive' (sent) — you send yourself under another's command.

words.definition: Willing to go along with rules, requests, or the wishes of others.
words.example: The compliant employee signed every form without a single protest.
words.mnemonic: Picture a 'comply-ant' — an ant that always complies with the colony.

words.definition: Willing to follow orders and do what one is told.
words.example: The obedient dog sat the instant its owner raised a hand.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'audire' (to hear) — you hear the command and heed it.

words.definition: Quiet, gentle, and unwilling to argue or assert oneself.
words.example: Too meek to complain, he ate the cold soup in silence.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'weak' — too weak-willed to ever push back.

words.definition: Easily managed and willing to do whatever one is asked.
words.example: The biddable intern rearranged the entire office without a word of complaint.
words.mnemonic: From 'bid' — a biddable person does whatever you bid them do.

words.definition: Easily bent physically, or readily influenced and shaped by others.
words.example: The pliant willow branch curved in the wind without ever snapping.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'plicare' (to fold) — like 'ply', it folds without breaking.

words.definition: Flexible enough to bend with ease, or readily persuaded to change.
words.example: The pliable copper wire twisted neatly around the fence post.
words.mnemonic: 'pli-' (fold) + '-able' — quite literally able to be folded.

words.definition: Lying flat on one's back, or passively failing to take action.
words.example: He lay supine on the grass, gazing up at the drifting clouds.
words.mnemonic: Hides 'up' and 'spine' — face up, spine flat against the ground.

words.definition: Lying stretched out face-down, often in submission, grief, or exhaustion.
words.example: The pilgrims fell prostrate before the altar, foreheads pressed to the stone.
words.mnemonic: 'pro-' (forward) + '-strate' (stretched) — stretched forward flat on the earth.

words.definition: Extremely hopeless, wretched, or degrading, often to a humiliating degree.
words.example: They lived in abject poverty, with barely a crust of bread to share.
words.mnemonic: 'ab-' (away) + '-ject' (thrown) — thrown away, cast down to the lowest state.

words.definition: To crouch or shrink back in fear of something threatening.
words.example: The puppy began to cower under the table at the first crack of thunder.
words.mnemonic: Hides 'cow' — a scaredy-cow shrinking away and trembling.

words.definition: To recoil or wince in embarrassment, disgust, or fearful submission.
words.example: She cringed as the singer hit yet another painfully flat note.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'hinge' — you fold inward at the hinge in discomfort.

words.definition: To act submissively toward a more powerful person in order to gain favor.
words.example: He would truckle to his boss, praising every idea no matter how foolish it was.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'knuckle under' — you truckle when you knuckle under to someone stronger.

words.definition: To give way to another person's wishes or judgment out of respect.
words.example: On questions of law, I always defer to my attorney's greater experience.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'ferre' (to carry): you carry the decision over to someone you respect.

words.definition: Polite respect that leads you to accept another's wishes or judgment.
words.example: Out of deference to the elderly guests, the band kept the volume low all evening.
words.mnemonic: The '-ence' noun of defer: the quiet state of giving way to someone.

words.definition: To stop resisting something overpowering and give in to it.
words.example: After hours of staring at the pastries, she finally succumbed and bought a dozen.
words.mnemonic: Latin sub + cumbere, 'to lie down under' — you lie down under the pressure.

words.definition: To give way to pressure, force, or persuasion.
words.example: The rusty gate finally yielded when he threw his full weight against it.
words.mnemonic: A red 'YIELD' road sign tells you to give way to oncoming traffic.

words.definition: To choke someone by squeezing the throat, or to strangle an activity.
words.example: Enraged, he grabbed the pickpocket by the collar as if to throttle him.
words.mnemonic: 'Throttle' hides the word 'throat' — you grab the throat.

words.definition: To prevent a person or animal from speaking or making noise.
words.example: Critics accused the regime of muzzling the press with harsh new censorship laws.
words.mnemonic: Picture the strap 'muzzle' over a dog's snout so it can't bark or bite.

words.definition: To restrict someone's freedom, often with metal restraints on the limbs.
words.example: The prisoners were shackled together as they shuffled toward the courtyard.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'shake + ankle' — chains rattling and shaking around your ankles.

words.definition: To confine or restrain, especially by binding the feet with chains.
words.example: Crushing debt fettered the young couple, keeping them from ever moving away.
words.mnemonic: 'Fetter' sounds like 'feet-er' — chains made for the feet.

words.definition: To confine a person's hands with metal rings joined by a chain.
words.example: The guards manacled his wrists before leading him out of the holding cell.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'manus' (hand) — restraints made for the hands.

words.definition: To restrict or hinder someone's freedom of action or movement.
words.example: She refused to let outdated rules trammel her ambition, breaking every convention that stood in her way.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'tram' + 'shackle' — picture a tram car chained to its rails, unable to leave the tracks.

words.definition: To slow down or get in the way of someone's progress or effort.
words.example: Heavy rain hampered the rescue team as they climbed the muddy slope.
words.mnemonic: Imagine tripping over a picnic 'hamper' basket that slows your every step.

words.definition: To limit, control, or reduce something so it stays within bounds.
words.example: She learned to curb her spending after the credit card bill arrived.
words.mnemonic: Sound-alike: the raised curb at the road's edge stops a car from rolling onto the sidewalk.

words.definition: To hold back or keep under control by force or self-discipline.
words.example: Two officers had to restrain the man as he lunged toward the stage.
words.mnemonic: Hear 're-strain': you strain against a leash to hold a bolting dog back.

words.definition: To bring under control, or to react with sudden anger and offense.
words.example: He bridled at the suggestion that his work had been careless.
words.mnemonic: A bridle is the head-harness that lets a rider rein a horse in — control it.

words.definition: To bring a force or resource under control and put it to productive use.
words.example: Engineers built the dam to harness the river's power for electricity.
words.mnemonic: A harness straps a horse to a plow so its strength can be put to work.

words.definition: A large farm animal kept for its milk or meat, female of cattle.
words.example: The farmer rose at dawn to milk the cow before the pails were needed.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like the 'COW' it says — 'moo' from a mouth shaped like a round 'cow' O.

words.definition: To pressure or frighten someone using harsh, domineering language.
words.example: The lawyer tried to browbeat the witness into changing her testimony.
words.mnemonic: Brow + beat: someone furrows their brow and beats you down with words.

words.definition: To hurt, threaten, or coerce someone perceived as weaker.
words.example: The older kids bullied him until he handed over his lunch money.
words.mnemonic: Think of a 'bull' charging at smaller animals — throwing its weight around.

words.definition: To fill someone with fear in order to influence their behavior.
words.example: The towering bodyguard intimidated anyone who came near the door.
words.mnemonic: It hides the word 'timid' — you make the other person timid.

words.definition: To torment or nag someone with blustering, aggressive talk.
words.example: He hectored the waiter over every tiny mistake on the bill.
words.mnemonic: Named for Hector, the Trojan warrior who loudly taunted his enemies before battle.

words.definition: To force someone into action through coercion or pressure.
words.example: She was dragooned into organizing the entire office party.
words.mnemonic: Dragoons were armed cavalry who forced civilians to obey at gunpoint.

words.definition: To seize property forcibly, often for military or official use.
words.example: The soldiers commandeered every truck in the village overnight.
words.mnemonic: A 'commander' who takes whatever he wants: command-eer.

words.definition: To seize power, a position, or a right without legal authority.
words.example: The general usurped the throne while the king lay ill.
words.mnemonic: 'You-slurp' up power that was never yours to take.

words.definition: To hold and use a weapon, tool, or influence with skill.
words.example: The blacksmith wielded his heavy hammer with practiced ease.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'field': a warrior on the field wields a sword.

words.definition: To wave or display something, especially a weapon, in a threatening way.
words.example: He brandished a knife and demanded the money from the register.
words.mnemonic: 'Brand' + flourish: waving a burning brand (torch) around your head.

words.definition: To prove stronger and win out in the end, or to be widespread.
words.example: After years in court, justice finally prevailed for the family.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'avail': your effort avails, so you come out on top.

words.definition: Standing above all others in a field through outstanding quality or importance.
words.example: For decades she was the preeminent cardiac surgeon in the country, sought out even by heads of state.
words.mnemonic: Break it down: pre- ('before') + eminent — someone ranked even ahead of the merely eminent.

words.definition: More important than anything else; ranking above every other concern.
words.example: In the operating room, patient safety is paramount, overriding both cost and convenience.
words.mnemonic: 'Para-mount' — pictured as sitting above the mountain; nothing else rises higher.

words.definition: Highest in authority, rank, power, or degree; above all others.
words.example: The Supreme Court's ruling ended the dispute, since no higher body could overturn it.
words.mnemonic: A 'supreme' pizza has everything piled on top — supreme means topmost.

words.definition: The condition of holding the greatest power, authority, or status.
words.example: Naval supremacy let the empire control every major trade route in the region.
words.mnemonic: Add -acy ('state of') to 'supreme' — the state of being on top.

words.definition: Rising toward greater power, popularity, or influence.
words.example: With the old guard fading, the young reformers were clearly ascendant within the party.
words.mnemonic: 'Ascend' + -ant — one that is climbing upward, like a rising star.

words.definition: A position of dominant control or governing influence over others.
words.example: After the merger, the founders lost their ascendancy to the incoming board.
words.mnemonic: You ascend to the top, then hold the -ancy — the state of ruling from up there.

words.definition: Most frequent, noticeable, or powerful within a group or setting.
words.example: Pine is the predominant tree here, crowding out nearly every other species.
words.mnemonic: Pre- + 'dominate' — it dominates the scene before anything else even shows up.

words.definition: The fact of being first in order, rank, or significance.
words.example: Medieval scholars endlessly debated the primacy of faith over reason.
words.mnemonic: The root 'prim-' means first (as in 'primary') — being number one.

words.definition: A system in which people or things are ranked in graded levels of status.
words.example: In the corporate hierarchy, every intern reported upward through five layers of managers.
words.mnemonic: 'Hier-' (sacred) + '-archy' (rule): originally the ranked orders of angels, now any ranked layers.

words.definition: A particular level of authority or status within an organized group.
words.example: She climbed into the upper echelon of the firm within just five years.
words.mnemonic: French for 'rung of a ladder' — say 'ash-uh-lon' and picture each rung as a level.

words.definition: Extremely harsh, cruel, or severe, especially regarding rules or punishment.
words.example: The draconian curfew jailed anyone caught outdoors after eight o'clock.
words.mnemonic: Named for Draco, the ancient Athenian lawmaker whose penalties were brutally severe.

words.definition: The right or ability to govern oneself and make one's own decisions.
words.example: The region was granted autonomy, running its own schools, courts, and budget.
words.mnemonic: 'Auto-' (self) + '-nomy' (rule/law) — making your own laws.

words.definition: Acting or existing independently, without outside control.
words.example: The autonomous rover navigated the crater with no commands from Earth.
words.mnemonic: 'Auto-' (self) + '-nomous' (governed) — a self-driving car is autonomous.

words.definition: Formal, sworn loyalty and duty owed to a superior or a cause.
words.example: The knight knelt before the throne and swore fealty to his new king.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'fee' + 'loyalty' — a vassal paid his fee and pledged loyalty.

words.definition: A gesture or attitude of deep respect and submission toward someone.
words.example: The courtiers made deep obeisance as the emperor swept past them.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'obey' hidden inside obeisance — you bow to those you obey.
